slides.text:
Observed behavior : the deployed commit is not the reviewed commit, yet git diff between the two is empty
Git state         : two commit objects with the same tree and the same parent; the branch points at the newer one
Mechanism         : an amend, a rebase or a cherry-pick wrote a new commit object with a new committer line
Root cause        : the commit ID is the hash of the commit object, and the committer time is part of that object
Why Git does this : an ID that covers every byte lets any two repositories agree on history by comparing IDs alone
Correct fix       : prove equal content with git rev-parse X^{tree} Y^{tree}; then move the branch back to X or re-approve Y
Prevention        : do not rewrite a commit after review or deployment; gate deploys on the approved ID, not on a branch name

# Each call changes exactly one input of the call above.
mk "$T" "$T" HEAD~1 'Add F1 metric.' 'HEAD^{tree}'                 # message: one more character
mk '@1788755641 +0530' "$T" HEAD~1 'Add F1 metric' 'HEAD^{tree}'   # author date: one second later
mk "$T" '@1788755641 +0530' HEAD~1 'Add F1 metric' 'HEAD^{tree}'   # committer date: one second later
mk '@1788755640 +0000' "$T" HEAD~1 'Add F1 metric' 'HEAD^{tree}'   # author time zone: same instant,
mk "$T" "$T" HEAD 'Add F1 metric' 'HEAD^{tree}'                    # parent: HEAD instead of HEAD~1
mk "$T" "$T" HEAD~1 'Add F1 metric' 'HEAD~1^{tree}'                # tree: the previous snapshot
GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL=You@example.com mk "$T" "$T" HEAD~1 'Add F1 metric' 'HEAD^{tree}'   # author email:

slides.body: So here's your answer for the CTO.
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Saying "I only fixed the message, the code is the same commit". Root cause: the message is part of the commit object, and the ID is the hash of that object; it is the same tree and a different commit.
Concluding from two different IDs that the code differs. Root cause: the ID covers metadata too; compare X^{tree} and Y^{tree} to compare content.
Expecting .git/HEAD to change on a commit. Root cause: the commit sets the ref that HEAD names; HEAD itself still holds the branch name.
Committing on the wrong branch, or on none. Root cause: nothing in a commit says which branch it is on; it goes wherever HEAD pointed, so check git status before you commit, not after.
Storing abbreviated IDs in deploy records. Root cause: a prefix that is unique today can become ambiguous later.

slides.body: Now, out of the lab. An evaluation run is tracked with the commit ID of the code.
The remedy it gives: record git rev-parse HEAD together with git status --porcelain, or refuse a tracked run when that output is not empty.
And for deployments, the prevention line of the root-cause box: gate deploys on the approved ID, not on a branch name.

beats.text: Inside .git: one object per commit in the object database, Git's store of objects. Nothing else describes a commit. There's no table of commits and no per-branch list. A branch reaches its commits by following parent IDs from its tip.

beats.text: How git commit creates a commit. In one sentence: git commit turns the index into tree objects, wraps the top tree in a new commit object whose parent is the current HEAD commit, and moves the current branch to that object. It is 🟢 SAFE. The index is the middle box, and HEAD is the commit you're on.
beats.tele: How `git commit` creates a commit. In one sentence: `git commit` turns the index into tree objects, wraps the top tree in a new commit object whose parent is the current HEAD commit, and moves the current branch to that object. It is 🟢 SAFE. The index is the middle box, and HEAD is the commit you're on.

beats.text: Six steps, in the order in which their results depend on each other.
beats.tele: Six steps, in the order in which their results depend on each other.

beats.text: One, content: the index is the proposed snapshot.
beats.tele: One, content: the index is the proposed snapshot.

beats.text: Two, checks and message: the pre-commit hook runs before the message is obtained, and the commit-msg hook can reject the message. A hook is a script Git runs at a set moment. --no-verify skips both.
beats.tele: Two, checks and message: the `pre-commit` hook runs before the message is obtained, and the `commit-msg` hook can reject the message. A hook is a script Git runs at a set moment. `--no-verify` skips both.

beats.text: Three, trees: Git builds one tree per directory from the index entries. A tree that the object database already holds keeps its ID, and nothing new is stored. git write-tree performs this step alone.
beats.tele: Three, trees: Git builds one tree per directory from the index entries. A tree that the object database already holds keeps its ID, and nothing new is stored. `git write-tree` performs this step alone.

beats.text: Four, parent: the commit that HEAD resolves to becomes the parent. A first commit has none. A merge in progress adds the commits in MERGE_HEAD.
beats.tele: Four, parent: the commit that HEAD resolves to becomes the parent. A first commit has none. A merge in progress adds the commits in `MERGE_HEAD`.

beats.text: Five, the commit object: tree ID, parent IDs, author, committer and message are written as one object. Its hash is the commit ID.
beats.tele: Five, the commit object: tree ID, parent IDs, author, committer and message are written as one object. Its hash is the commit ID.

beats.text: Six, refs: the ref that HEAD names is set to the new ID, and the reflogs of HEAD and of the branch each gain a line. A reflog is Git's local journal of where a ref has pointed.
beats.tele: Six, refs: the ref that HEAD names is set to the new ID, and the reflogs of HEAD and of the branch each gain a line. A reflog is Git's local journal of where a ref has pointed.

beats.text: The state table: the working tree is unchanged, the current branch ref is set to the new commit, and the remote and GitHub are unchanged. In detached HEAD, HEAD itself is set to the new commit ID, and no branch moves.
beats.tele: The state table: the working tree is unchanged, the current branch ref is set to the new commit, and the remote and GitHub are unchanged. In detached HEAD, HEAD itself is set to the new commit ID, and no branch moves.

beats.text: Nothing in a commit says which branch it is on. It goes wherever HEAD pointed when you ran the command.
beats.tele: Nothing in a commit says which branch it is on. It goes wherever HEAD pointed when you ran the command.

beats.text: The commit ID. In one sentence: a commit ID is the hash of the commit object, so one ID names the snapshot, the metadata and, through the parent IDs, the whole history behind the commit.
beats.tele: The commit ID. In one sentence: a commit ID is the hash of the commit object, so one ID names the snapshot, the metadata and, through the parent IDs, the whole history behind the commit.

beats.text: Precisely: Git hashes the bytes commit, a space, the size, one NUL byte, and the object content. With the default object format the hash is SHA-1 and the ID has 40 hexadecimal digits. A SHA-256 repository has 64.
beats.tele: Precisely: Git hashes the bytes `commit`, a space, the size, one NUL byte, and the object content. With the default object format the hash is SHA-1 and the ID has 40 hexadecimal digits. A SHA-256 repository has 64.

beats.text: Two properties follow. Same bytes, same ID, on any machine. The replays in this course pin the identity and the clock, which is the only reason your IDs can equal the printed ones.
beats.tele: Two properties follow. Same bytes, same ID, on any machine. The replays in this course pin the identity and the clock, which is the only reason your IDs can equal the printed ones.

beats.text: And any change, new ID. The parent line contains the parent's ID, so an ID depends on every ancestor. Nobody can alter an old commit without changing the ID of every commit after it.
beats.tele: And any change, new ID. The `parent` line contains the parent's ID, so an ID depends on every ancestor. Nobody can alter an old commit without changing the ID of every commit after it.

beats.text: What the ID does not guarantee. It says nothing about who really wrote the commit. Author and committer are assertions: --author, the configuration and the environment accept any text. Only a verified signature is evidence of who created a commit. And an ID names the commit, and nothing outside it: a run started from a working tree with uncommitted edits executed code that no commit ID describes.

Git prints abbreviations whose length it computes from the size of the repository, seven characters in these sandboxes. A prefix that is unique today can become ambiguous later, so deploy records and model cards should store the full ID.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy: an entry in a ledger whose page numbers are computed from what is written on the page. Each entry points at a full inventory sheet, cites the page number of the entry before it, and names who did the work and who entered it. Change one character, and the page number changes.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Saying "I only fixed the message, the code is the same commit". Root cause: the message is part of the commit object, and the ID is the hash of that object; it is the same tree and a different commit.
beats.tele: Saying "I only fixed the message, the code is the same commit". Root cause: the message is part of the commit object, and the ID is the hash of that object; it is the same tree and a different commit.

beats.text: Concluding from two different IDs that the code differs. Root cause: the ID covers metadata too; compare X^{tree} and Y^{tree} to compare content.
beats.tele: Concluding from two different IDs that the code differs. Root cause: the ID covers metadata too; compare `X^{tree}` and `Y^{tree}` to compare content.

beats.text: Expecting .git/HEAD to change on a commit. Root cause: the commit sets the ref that HEAD names; HEAD itself still holds the branch name.
beats.tele: Expecting `.git/HEAD` to change on a commit. Root cause: the commit sets the ref that HEAD names; HEAD itself still holds the branch name.

beats.text: Committing on the wrong branch, or on none. Root cause: nothing in a commit says which branch it is on; it goes wherever HEAD pointed, so check git status before you commit, not after.
